habitat: Cave salamanders inhabit limestone cave systems, rocky ravines, and moist forest floors throughout the Appalachian Mountains and Interior Low Plateau of the eastern United States, from Illinois and Indiana south to Alabama and Georgia. They are found at cave entrances, in the twilight zone (where light penetrates), along underground streams, and under rocks near springs and seeps. They require consistently cool, humid environments with stable temperatures (10-15°C) and high humidity (90-100%). Unlike true troglobites, they retain functional eyes and pigment, capable of surviving both in and out of caves.
diet: Cave salamanders are carnivorous, feeding on a variety of small invertebrates including insects, spiders, millipedes, mites, snails, and earthworms. In cave environments, they prey on cave crickets, springtails, isopods, and other arthropods adapted to subterranean life. They use olfactory cues and motion detection to locate prey in low-light conditions. They are primarily nocturnal foragers on the forest floor near cave entrances, retreating deeper into caves during dry periods or when surface temperatures are extreme.
behavior: Cave salamanders are among the most agile and active of all salamander species. They are excellent climbers, using their long, prehensile tail for balance on vertical rock faces — they can ascend nearly smooth limestone walls. Unlike many salamanders, they are often observed walking rather than crawling. They are territorial and may engage in tail-lashing displays when competing for prime foraging positions. Breeding occurs in underground pools and streams throughout much of the year. Females attach eggs individually to the underside of submerged rocks.
facts: Cave salamanders are one of the longest and most slender salamanders in North America, reaching lengths of 15-20 cm — over half of which is tail. Their brilliant orange to reddish-orange coloration, speckled with black spots, makes them one of the most beautiful salamanders. Unlike true cave species, they are not blind or depigmented — they frequently emerge to forage on the forest floor at night. They can live over 10 years. They are sensitive to water quality changes, serving as indicators of groundwater health in karst ecosystems.
naming: Cave salamander names might reflect their underground habitat or brilliant orange color. Consider names like Ember, Cavey, Grotto, Stalactite, Amber, Torch, Cavern, Spark, Limestone, Marble, or Vesper.
